column2: Then, lifting the pot, preceded by the recitation of blessings, the guru should sprinkle the disciple on the head, moving clockwise.
First uttering the pranava seven times and then the five Brahman mantras, at the end of the sprinkling he should encircle him with the conch water.
Then, showing a lovely lamp and wiping him with a cloth, he should dress him in a new string, loincloth and two garments.
His feet washed and having sipped water twice, wearing ash, the guru should take the newly born disciple by both hands in the middle of the pavilion,
Suta said: You are blessed, devotees of Mahadeva, benefactors of the world; hear, all you sages, the dialogue of those two again.
facing east, longing for the knowledge of his own true nature; seated on his own seat, the guru should say to him, "Be pure of soul."
And the guru, steady in the conviction "I am full, I am Shiva," should enter samadhi properly for a muhurta, his mind withdrawn.
Afterwards, opening his eyes, with a well-disposed mind, calmly he should look at the pure disciple standing with folded hands.
Placing his own hand smeared with ash on the disciple's head, he should teach clearly into his right ear: "Hamsah so'ham."
The meaning of the first word 'I' is Shiva himself, of the nature of Shakti; contemplate your own self: 'I am he, I am Shiva.'
Having taught the true meaning of the particle "yah," he should then respectfully explain the purport of the subsidiary sayings.
I shall tell you the sayings, O brahmin; listen with an attentive mind and hold them in your heart — so he should say clearly.
Hearing the words of Mahesha's son, which destroy duality and produce the knowledge of non-duality, the great sage was content.
Having bowed to and praised in many ways Kartikeya, Shiva's son, the great sage again asked about the truth with humility.
Hearing this, Kartikeya, pondering Vamadeva's words and thinking in his mind of Shiva and Shiva's consort, began to explain.
Beginning with the supporting Shakti, according to the rule stated for worship, he should invoke the god by the path of the five enclosures and worship him.
Having smeared that ash on his limbs according to rule, the guru should then seat him comfortably on the prepared seat.
Vamadeva said: Blessed one, knower of all truths, six-faced ocean of nectar, how do these ascetics of cultivated self become gurus,
by whose power the attainment of enjoyment, liberation and the like is accomplished for beings? Without the succession of teachers they have no right to teach.
And how are the tonsure and the bath of such a kind? Instruct me, master; please cut away my doubt.
Salutations to Shri Ganesha.
Salutations to Shri Gauri and Shankara.
The glorious Shiva Mahapurana.

Om, salutation to Shiva. The sixth book, the Kailasa Samhita, chapter 19: the description of the rite of the yoga-patta. Subrahmanya said: (1) Consciousness is Brahman. (2) I am Brahman. (3) That thou art. (4) This self is Brahman. (5) All this is to be dwelt in by the Lord. (6) I am breath. (7) The self of consciousness. (8) What is here is there; what is there is here. (9) It is other than the known and above the unknown. (10) This is your self, the inner controller, the immortal. (11) He who is in the person and he who is in the sun are one. (12) I am the supreme Brahman, higher than the high and the low. (13) Through the authority of Veda, shastra and guru, it is itself of the nature of bliss. (14) The Brahman abiding in all beings — that am I, without doubt. (15) I am the breath of the principle; I am the breath of the earth. (16) I am the breath of the waters, and I am the breath of fire. (17) I am the breath of the wind, and I am the breath of space. (18) I am the breath of the three qualities. (19) I am all, I am the self of all, the transmigrant; what has been, what will be and what is — because I am the self of all, I am without a second. (20) All this indeed is Brahman. (21) I am all, I am free. (22) He who is that, he am I; the swan, he am I.

Now he states the meaning of the great sayings. The meaning of the saying "Consciousness is Brahman" has already been explained; the meaning of the word "I" is the supreme Lord, of the nature of Shakti.
How it is so, I shall explain here; listen, O sage. The word "known," as before, is not used in its ordinary sense;
it proceeds beyond the known and likewise beyond the unknown; it is settled that it is other and could not be accomplished otherwise.
This is your self, the inner controller, who is immortal, is Shiva himself — Shambhu who is in the person and who abides in the sun.
He and "that one" suggest separateness, yet all is declared to be he; its meaning with two limiting adjuncts is stated figuratively.
The Shrutis call that lord Shambhu golden; "golden-armed" indicates his whole body.
Otherwise his lordship would not hold. In the Chhandogya, Shambhu Shiva is heard of as "he who is within."
Likewise with golden beard and golden hair — from the nails to the tips of the hair he is golden throughout.
I am the supreme Brahman, higher than the high and the low — I shall tell the purport of this saying; listen to it.
The meaning of the word "I" is declared to be Shiva of the nature of Shakti; the saying's meaning is surely the joining "I am he."
The letter a, foremost of all letters, is the light, the supreme Shiva; the letter h is of the form of space, declared to be of the nature of Shakti.
Rudra, Brahma and Vishnu are declared by the Shruti itself, not otherwise; and the god supreme above them is indicated by the word "para."
Through the disciple's practice of the sayings of Veda, shastra and gurus, Shambhu, full of perfect bliss, becomes manifest in his heart.
Shambhu abides in all beings; he am I, without doubt. I am the breath of the whole host of principles; I am Shiva.
Having said this, Shiva says again, of the three principles: in "I am the breath," by taking in everything from earth to the qualities, O sage,
contemplate that all the Atma principles are included; and again the taking of all, in the Vidya principle, of Shiva and the self.
I am the breath of the two principles; I am all, the self of all. Being the inner controller of the individual self, I am always that individual self.
What has been, what is to be, what will be — all of it; because it is made of me, I am all, and "all indeed is Rudra" too,
says the Shruti, O sage, which came forth directly from Shiva's mouth. The self of all, through constant union with these supreme qualities,
since there is no supreme self apart from myself, I alone am without a second. The meaning of the saying "All this indeed is Brahman" was stated earlier.
From the union of Shiva and Shakti bliss constantly arises; "Brahman" clearly means the all-selfhood of Shiva and Shakti.
That Shambhu who is the self of all — he am I, the swan; I am Shiva. This, Vamadeva, is the meaning of all the sayings as told by Shiva.
Thus the guru should respectfully teach the disciple the meaning taught by the Lord's Shruti sayings, which directly grants men oneness with Shiva.
Taking the conch with its stand, purifying it with the astra mantra and ash, and placing it before him on the worshipped square,
worshipping it with "Om" and with fragrance and the like, adorned with cloth, filling it with scented water and worshipping it with the mantra "Om,"
and consecrating it seven times with the pranava — "Whoever makes even the slightest separation is subject to great fear,"
so says the Shruti, the true principle; be firm of soul and free of fear. Having said this, he should himself worship the disciple, meditating on him as the god.
Worshipping the disciple's seat by the path of the six raisings, conceiving it as Shiva's seat, he should imagine the form of Shiva.
Placing the five Brahmans from head to feet, and also the kalas of the pranava with the distinctions of head, face and kala,
the thirty-eight in the form of mantras, on the disciple's body and head, invoking Shiva, he should show the gestures of installation and the rest.
What was taught earlier — "I am he" — should be contemplated. In "That thou art," the meaning of the word "that" has been explained.
Offering sweet rice as food offering with "Om" and "svaha," and in order water for rinsing and sipping, arghya, incense, lamp and the rest,
having worshipped with the eight names together with brahmins versed in the Veda, he should recite "The knower of Brahman attains," "Bhrigu, son of Varuna," and so on,
from "He who among the gods" to "He who is supreme is Maheshvara"; before him, taking a garland made of white lilies and the like,
rising, he should slowly recite the Siddhiskandha in the shastra composed by Shri Virupaksha, in the five-faced form,
up to "Khyati, I am full"; with a well-disposed mind the teacher should then place the garland around the disciple's neck.
Then he should have a tilaka made with sandal paste, and the whole body anointed again, according to his own tradition and the rule.
Then the teacher lovingly should give him a name ending in "Shripada," and an umbrella and sandals, with the arrangement of durva grass,
and the right to expound, the rites and the rest, and the acceptance of the guru's seat; thus favouring that disciple who is Shiva in form,
he should say to him, "Always abide in samadhi as 'I am Shiva,'" and then himself bow down to him.

Otherwise, in "I am he," there would be a contrary contemplation of meaning: the word "I" is masculine, and "that" would be neuter; thus, being mutually opposed, the two could not be construed together.
When the disciple has thus been saluted, the guru himself should instruct him, of good conduct, restrained in speech, standing bowed in humility:

From today be devoted to showing grace to the worlds. Examine a disciple for a year and accept him according to rule.
shivpurana:10:19.53	Abandon passion and other faults and be devoted to meditation on Shiva. Keep company with those accomplished in the true tradition, and not with others.
shivpurana:10:19.54	Never eat without worshipping Shiva, as long as life lasts. Holding to devotion to the guru, be happy, be happy.
In this way the excellent guru, compassionate, an ocean of knowledge, should deal with the disciple with a well-disposed mind.
Out of affection for you, Vamadeva, lord of sages, I have told you the manner of the yoga-patta, though it is most secret.
Having said this, the six-faced one lovingly began to describe to him, out of compassion for ascetics, the auspicious order of the rite of tonsure and bathing.
and the cause of the world of female and male forms would be otherwise. "He, that thou art" — such is the contemplation of the teaching's meaning.
It is other than the known and also above the unknown — in this saying there is also the contemplation of the opposite of the result.
He is declared to be the highest of all, the self of all, the supreme Brahman; the high, the low, and higher than the highest — thus threefold.
I am full, being of the nature of being; I alone am ever free. The bound souls, by my grace, are freed, having taken refuge in my state.
Then, placing the limbs in order with "sarvajnani" and the rest, he should arrange the sixteen services beginning with the seat.
Others should likewise bow according to their tradition. Then the disciple should rise and bow to the guru, to the guru's guru, and to the disciples of his own guru.
In the saying "This self," the pair of words is masculine in form. "All this world is to be dwelt in by the Lord," since it must be protected by the Lord.
The self of consciousness; "What is here is there" — one should reflect that "he is the same," so it is said here by the learned who hold the doctrine.
And in the saying above, "he who is there abides here" — the meaning, as before, is the Person, as held by the wise.
Salutations to Shri Ganesha.
Salutations to Shri Gauri and Shankara.
The glorious Shiva Mahapurana.

Om, salutation to Shiva. The sixth book, the Kailasa Samhita, chapter 20: the description of the rite of tonsure and bathing. Subrahmanya said: I shall tell you the rite of tonsure and bathing, Vamadeva, great sage, by which, when properly performed, the ascetic at once attains supreme purity.
Taking one portion of the clay there and having it given with the other hand, he should smear his hands twelve times and wash each with water.
Again, smearing one portion on the feet, another on the face and another on the hands in order, and washing with water, he should enter the water again.
Dividing another portion of clay, he should smear it on the head twelve times in order, and up to the face, and plunge in again and again.
Going to the bank, he should take sixteen mouthfuls of water and sip twice; restraining the breath again, repeating the pranava sixteen times,
dividing another portion of clay into three, with one he should cleanse the waist and the feet and sip water twice.
Then, restraining the breath sixteen times with the pranava, silent, he should place another portion on his thigh in three parts, saying "Om,"
sprinkle and consecrate it seven times; once on the palms of his hands, smearing it thrice, he should then look at the purifying form of the sun.
Smearing both armpits with his hands crossed, with another portion of clay, the wise disciple, firm of mind,
taking another portion of pure clay, devoted to his guru, should smear himself from head to feet with his eyes on the sun.
Having received the rite of the yoga-patta, lord of sages, that disciple, observing his vow completely, should prepare for the tonsure.
Then the disciple should devoutly remember Shiva with Amba, the great lord, Shankara, the moon-crested, master of all lordship.
He should lovingly bow three times with the eight limbs to the guru, who is Shiva, and once with the five limbs, and rising, salute him.
Entering the holy water, plunging and rising in its midst, placing that clay on his shoulder, he should smear himself in the way described before.
Gathering what remains there and entering the water, mixing it well there and smearing it on all his limbs,
uttering "Om" three times, remembering Shiva's lotus feet — for he, by rule, always carries one across the ocean of worldly existence —
sprinkling with "Om" water mixed with the ash of the Viraja fire, wiping his limbs, he should then bathe well with ash.
Then he should make the auspicious tripundra according to the stated rule, on all the stated limbs, carefully, O sage.
Then, pure in mind, he should perform the midday rites, bowing to Maheshvara, the gurus, the holy places and the rest.
He should worship Maheshana with supreme devotion, O sage — together with Ambika, the giver of knowledge, the protector of the three worlds.
Having bowed to the guru especially and received his leave, washing his head and sipping water, he should undergo the tonsure clothed.
Then, pure of soul, he should beg alms there as is fitting, arranged in five ways, avoiding tainted food.
Cleansing, bathing, begging and constant solitude — these four are the duties of a mendicant; there is no fifth.
A gourd, a bamboo vessel, a wooden one and a clay one — these are the four vessels of a mendicant; there is no fifth.
Betel, a metal vessel, emission of semen, white garments, sleeping by day and eating at night — these six are forbidden to ascetics.
Those who act contrary to the letter are remembered as rakshasas; therefore an ascetic should never act contrary to it.
The ascetic should carefully perform the tonsure and bath for purity, remembering in his mind the pure supreme Brahman, Sadashiva.
Thus, tiger among sages, out of affection for you I have told you the whole rite of tonsure and bathing; what more do you wish to hear?
Afterwards he should wash the garment and the razor and the rest with clay and water, and smearing the barber's hands with clay, give him clay, saying "Wash."
Placing them and sprinkling them with water, saying "Shiva, Shiva," covering his own eyes with the ring finger and thumb consecrated,
opening them with the astra mantra and looking at the razor and other means of tonsure, he should consecrate them twelve times and sprinkle them with the astra mantra.
Placing the clay in a pure spot, dividing it into three, and again making it threefold, he should sprinkle it and consecrate it with the astra mantra.
Then, rising and taking his staff, on the ground he should devoutly remember his own guru, the giver of the mantra, established in knowledge.
Then that ascetic, firm of mind, abiding in his own dharma, pure, should go for alms among the classes of brahmins and among good people.
Taking the razor, with the pranava he should cut on the right side; having some of the hair cut at the tips, he should have it all shaved.
Taking a leaf, he should not scatter it on the bare ground; he should have the beard and the nails of hands and feet cut.
Gathering clay at the foot of a bilva, ashvattha, tulasi or the like, and plunging twelve times into the water, going to the bank and sitting down,
Salutations to Shri Ganesha.
Salutations to Shri Gauri and Shankara.

The glorious Shiva Mahapurana, book 6, chapter 21: the description of the rites for ascetics after death up to the tenth day. Vamadeva said: For ascetics who are liberated there is no cremation; I have heard that when the body dies it is buried.
Doing that, the ascetic should be properly devoted to meditation on Shiva, O sage, as a rule always, his mind attached to the pranava.
If, through the weakness of the body, the ascetic cannot hold steady, then, free of desire and remembering Shiva, he should give up his worn-out body.
By the grace of Sadashiva, O sage, impelled by Nandi, five renowned deities in the form of conductors come.
One has the form of fire, a body made of a mass of light; one presides over the day, one presides over the bright fortnight,
and one has the form of the northern course — five intent on grace. Smoke, darkness, night, the one presiding over the dark fortnight,
and the one of the form of the southern course — these are the five renowned deities. Hear now of their workings, Vamadeva, great sage.
Those five deities take beings devoted to the performance of rites and go to heaven by the power of their merit, O sage.
Having enjoyed the pleasures described, when their merit is exhausted, they return to the human world and take birth as before.
The others again divide the path in five, and beginning from the earth, in the order of fire and the rest, lead the ascetic to the state of Sadashiva.
Tell me that rite lovingly, Kartikeya, my guru; there is no other in the three worlds who can tell it besides you.
Seeing him arrived, Sadashiva, god of gods, if he is dispassionate, teaches him the purport of the great mantra,
gives him a body like his own, consecrates him as a leader of ganas, and so Shankara, lord of all, leader of all, shows him grace:
adorned with the deer, the axe, the excellent trident and the boon-giving gesture, three-eyed, bearing the crescent moon and matted locks gleaming with the Ganga,
and he grants him the finest celestial chariot, all-going, granting all desires, surrounded by Rudra-maidens for one dispassionate toward the branches,
charming with the sounds of dancing, singing, drums and other instruments, adorned with divine garments, garlands, unguents and ornaments,
full of pots of divine nectar and filled with divine water, radiant as ten million suns, cool as ten million moons,
swift as the mind and all-going. When he has enjoyed pleasures and his curiosity for pleasure is exhausted,
the supreme Lord brings down upon him the most intense Shakti, most hard to reach by nature, radiant as the fire of dissolution, eager to burn the wilderness,
and grants him the purport of the great mantra, fixed and unwavering: "I am full, in the form of being; I am Shambhu."
Those who, resting in the sense of fullness, are freed from the cage of the body, and those who, freed from the body by the path of worship, have gone to the supreme —
At the end of the lotus-born's lifespan, the teacher of the world gives him the supreme liberation, free of return.
Therefore this very state, possessing the totality of all lordship, is also the bell-path of liberation; such is the conclusion of the Vedantas.
When that ascetic of the true tradition is dying and weak, ascetics should then stand around him out of kindness.
Then all of them there, in order, should teach him the pranava and the rest, and the sayings and their purport, with collected minds,
and describe them clearly and lovingly, always making him remember Shiva, the supreme light beyond qualities, bowing until he passes away.
For these the order of rites is said to be the same here; for those whose bodies are not given the rites, no evil fate arises.
Since they have renounced all rites and are devoted to taking refuge in Shiva, the kingdom of the king who defiles their body perishes,
and the dwellers of that village too become very miserable; therefore, to avert that fault, this procedure is stated.
He, humble in mind, should at that time recite the mantra from "namah irinyaya" to "namah amivatkebhyah."
and the special destinies of them, blessed son of Shankara — please tell me lovingly, considering me your own disciple.
Sons and others should properly perform the excellent rites. I shall tell them out of kindness, O brahmin; listen attentively.
Having worshipped the body, bathed it with pure water and worshipped it with flowers and the like, with the Shri Rudra and Chamaka and the Rudra Sukta in order,
placing a conch before it and sprinkling it with its water, putting a flower on the head, he should wipe it with the pranava.
Removing the loincloth and the rest, he should put on others, and then smear the whole body with ash according to rule.
Making the tripundra according to rule and a tilaka with sandal, he should adorn the body with flowers and garlands.
On the chest, throat, head, arms, forearms and ears in order he should adorn it with rudraksha garlands and ornaments, with mantras.
Having fumigated it well, raising it and placing it on a sling, he should set the body in a lovely chariot made of the five Brahmans.
With the five Brahman mantras beginning with Om, from Sadya on in order, he should adorn that chariot with fragrant flowers and garlands.
With dancing and music, and with the Vedic chanting of brahmins on all sides, he should circle the village clockwise and go on, bearing the dead one.
Suta said: Hearing the sage's request, the son of Shakti, slayer of the gods' foes, told that most secret thing that Bhrigu had heard from the Lord.
Digging a pit for the sacrifice to the god, the measure of a staff, sprinkling it with the pranava and the vyahritis and spreading it in order
with shami leaves and flowers, northward-pointing, and above them spreading darbha grass, a seat of cloth, deerskin and kusha,
he should sprinkle that body with the pranava, the Brahman mantras and the five products of the cow, and bathe it with the Raudra Sukta and the pranava;
bathing it with conch water, he should place a flower on the head. Devoted to the one departed and intent on remembering Shiva,
lifting it with "Om," preceded by the recitation of blessings, he should place it in the pit in the yoga posture, facing east as far as possible.
Adorning it with fragrance and flowers and with guggulu incense, saying "Vishnu, the oblation," and "Protect it," he should give
the staff into the right hand and the water-pot into the left, with water, with the mantra "Prajapati, none other than you."
Touching the head with the mantra "Brahma jajnanam prathamam," and reciting the Rudra Sukta, he should touch the space between the brows and recite.
With the four verses beginning "ma no mahantam," he should then split the head with a coconut and afterwards fill the pit.
Subrahmanya said: This very secret, O sage, was told directly by the blessed, all-knowing Pinaka-bearer to Bhrigu, the Shiva-yogi.
Having heard from the guru's mouth the knowledge of the meaning of the three words, born of the sayings of Vedanta and Agama, he should practise the yoga of restraint and the rest.
Having led them to the feet worthy of salutation, they stand behind the god of gods, forms of grace, employed only in their task.
granting samadhi and unobstructed powers, forms of his own servitude and vibration, the capacity for the work of the sun and others.
Reciting "Om" at the end, he should then fill the pit; then there is atonement for that fault, lord of sages.
Then all those ascetics, in the east or else in the north, in a holy place near a holy tree,
touching the spot with the five Brahman mantras, single-minded, he should recite "He who among the gods," "He who is supreme is Maheshvara."
Having thus recited, to Mahadeva with Amba, the medicine for worldly existence, all-knowing, dependent on none, bestowing grace on all,
he should make of clay a platform one aratni high and two aratnis wide, and plaster it with cow-dung.
In its centre, a square; he should worship with fragrance and rice grains, fragrant flowers, bilva leaves and tulasi.
Then with the pranava he should offer incense, lamp, milk and oblation; having given them, he should circumambulate and bow five times.
Repeating the pranava twelve times, he should then bow, and give the Brahma-arghya with the pranava in the order of the directions and intermediate directions.
Thus the rite up to the tenth day has been told to you; now, best of sages, hear the rite of the eleventh day for ascetics.
I shall tell it to you now, O brahmin; it is not to be given to just anyone, but to a disciple who is peaceful and endowed with devotion to Shiva.
If there is an ascetic established in samadhi who leaves his body in the state of Shiva, that most steadfast one becomes the full Shiva.
For one whose mind is unsteady and who does not attain samadhi, I shall tell the means; listen attentively.
Salutations to Shri Ganesha.
Salutations to Shri Gauri and Shankara.
The glorious Shiva Mahapurana.

Om, salutation to Shiva. The sixth book, the Kailasa Samhita, chapter 22: the description of the rites of the eleventh day for ascetics. Subrahmanya said: The rite declared for when the eleventh day arrives I shall tell you, tiger among sages, out of affection for you.
charming with three eyes and faces like the full moon, crowned with the crescent moon shining on ruby diadems,
their cheeks touched by earrings, with full, high breasts, charming with necklaces, armlets, bracelets and girdles,
slender-waisted, broad-hipped, clad in red divine garments, their lotus feet tinkling with ruby anklets, with toe-rings and hips most lovely and charming.
What can be accomplished by grace embodied, as by Shiva? Therefore everything is to be accomplished by the form that is Shakti, as by Mahesha.
The five forms have been adopted by the bestower of grace on all; divine, accomplishing all tasks, intent on the highest grace.
Having thus meditated on all those auspicious ones intent on grace, he should give water for their feet with drops of conch water,
water for sipping to their hands, and have arghya offered to their heads; and with drops of conch water he should imagine their bathing.
He should have divine red garments given with upper cloths, and give priceless crowns and other ornaments,
well-scented sandal, most beautiful unbroken grains, and fragrant, charming flowers.
Having swept and plastered the altar and performed the recitation for an auspicious day, sprinkling it, beginning in the west and ending in the east, five in order,
then, with "namah" at the end, he should give sweet rice soaked in honey, with ghee, sugar, cakes, bananas and jaggery,
each filled on a banana leaf and well-scented; saying "bhur bhuvah svah," he should have the sprinkling and the rest done.
Uttering "Om hrim," he should offer the food with "svaha," and saying "namah," offer drinking water with supreme love.
Then he should lovingly remove them, beginning from the east, best of sages; cleaning the spot, he should have water for rinsing, sipping and arghya given.
Having offered betel, incense and lamp, circumambulation and salutation, he should entreat them, placing his folded hands on his head:
May the holy Mothers, well pleased, declare this ascetic who seeks Shiva's state worthy of protection at the lotus feet of the supreme Lord.
Having thus entreated them all and dismissed them as they came, he should take their blessed food and have it given to maidens,
or to cows, or cast it into water, never otherwise. Here he should perform the parvana rite, never the ekoddishta for an ascetic.
I shall tell you the rule for the parvana shraddha here; hear it, best of sages, by which welfare comes from it.
facing north and standing himself, he should make the mandalas, measuring a span, and a square in the middle,
Resolving "I shall perform the parvana shraddha," he should place excellent darbha grass to the north for seats and touch water.
Inviting four brahmins who are devotees of Shiva and firm in their vows, anointed and bathed, he should devoutly seat them there,
saying, "Be gracious for the sake of the Vishvedevas," then "for the self," and also "for the inner self,"
and "for the supreme self"; saying thus and entreating them, the ascetic should with faith choose them truly and respectfully.
Washing their feet and seating them facing east, adorning them with fragrance and the like, he should feed them before Shiva.
Plastering the spot with cow-dung and spreading darbha grass with its tips to the east, with breath restrained, resolving on the offering of pindas,
saying "I shall perform it," and worshipping the three mandalas — the self, the inner self and the supreme self —
speaking them in the dative and then saying "this pinda," and "I give," he should give the pindas with devotion.
Then he should give kusha water according to rule, and rising, perform circumambulation and salutation.
in order, in the shapes of a point, a triangle, a hexagon and a circle; and placing a conch before him, by the path of the order stated for worship,
The rite of Vishnu's worship is prescribed everywhere for protection; he should perform a great worship of Vishnu and offer sweet rice.
Then, inviting twelve brahmins versed in the Veda, worshipping them as Keshava and the others with fragrance, flowers, grains and the like,
giving them sandals, umbrellas, garments and the like according to rule, he should satisfy them with great devotion and many auspicious words.
Spreading darbha grass pointing east, and saying "bhuh svaha, bhuvah..." preceded by the pranava, he should offer sweet rice as bali on the ground.
The proper rite of the eleventh day has been told by me, lord of sages; I shall tell the rite of the twelfth day — hear it attentively, O brahmin.
Restraining the breath, making the resolve and worshipping the queens of the gods, the five deities described before in the form of conductors,
putting aside the darbha grass to the north and touching water, beginning in the west by the path of the six raisings of the seat,

Subrahmanya said: On the twelfth day, rising at dawn, bathing and performing the daily rites, devotees of Shiva, ascetics, or brahmins dear to Shiva
Having given incense and lamp, the whole worship having been done, he should say "May it be complete," and rising, bow.
Spreading banana leaves as plates and purifying them with water, with pure rice, sweet rice, cakes, pulse and relishes,
giving the foods together with bananas, coconuts and jaggery, he should give the plates and seats separately, naming them in order.
Sprinkling around and sprinkling, saying "the oblation of Vishnu" and "Protect it," having them touch it with the hand, he should rise.
Offering the aposhana, he should entreat them thus: "May Sadashiva and the others be pleased and grant me boons."
Then reciting "ye devah," he should let fall grains; bowing and rising, he should say "May there be nectar everywhere."
Having said this and gratified them, reciting from "gananam tva" onward — the beginnings of the Vedas, the Rudra and Chamaka, the Rudra Sukta and the five —
at the end of the brahmins' meal, giving grains with the mantras, and the final aposhana, and the cleansing of hands, feet and mouth,
when they have sipped water, seating them comfortably on their seats and giving pure water, then camphor and the rest as stated,
he should invite and summon them at midday, bathed and pure, and devoutly feed them according to rule with many kinds of delicious, auspicious food.
satisfying them with circumambulation and salutation, he should receive their blessings; bowing again, he should pray for unwavering devotion to the guru.
May Sadashiva and the others, pleased, depart as they wish — thus dismissing them, he should follow them properly as far as the door.
Stopped by them, he should turn back and, together with the brahmins at the door, kinsmen, the poor and the helpless, eat and remain at ease.
Nothing will go wrong anywhere — truly, truly, again and again. Performing this excellent worship of the guru every year, he enjoys great pleasures here and attains the world of Shiva.

Suta said: Having thus spoken to his own disciple Shri Vamadeva, the excellent sage who had received grace, the great-souled god, best of the wise, serene in mind, having swiftly bestowed supreme grace,
what was told long ago to the lords of sages of the Naimisha forest by the lord of sages Vyasa — "therefore you are the first teacher, and he is renowned in the world as the second noble one."
Having heard it from your mouth, the lord of sages Sanatkumara, full of devotion to Shiva, told it to Vyasa; and that best of Shaivas, the perfect one, will tell it to Shuka.
Each of them, tiger among sages, has a group of four disciples, devoted to Vedic study and to establishing dharma.
Vaishampayana, Paila, Jaimini and Sumantu — these four are the mighty disciples of Vyasa.
In the presence of the supreme Lord, by the path of the five enclosures, he should seat them there and worship, restraining his breath, silent.
Sanaka, Sananda, then the sage Sanatana and Sanatsujata — these best of yogis, dear to Shiva,

are disciples of Sanatkumara, most learned in the meaning of all the Vedas. The guru, the supreme guru, then the guru higher than the highest, and the Parameshthi guru — these are to be worshipped by the yogi Shuka.
This knowledge of the pranava abides in the four groups; it is the highest source of all and in Kashi the cause of true liberation.

May this wondrous mandala, ever the seat of the supreme Shiva, supremely worshipful to the best of ascetics whose minds are full of the inquiry into Vedanta, enclosed by the great space and the rest arranged by the divisions of the Veda and so on, give you delight, and be the bringer of welfare and prosperity to the worlds.
This supreme secret spoken by Shiva, the highest, determined by the conclusions of Vedanta — since you have heard it from me, O sage, the wisest call it your doctrine.
Therefore the ascetic who goes to Shiva by this very path, "I am Shiva," becomes Shiva, for liberation from the divisions beginning with the Grandsire, as these rivers go to the ocean.
Suta said: Having thus taught this to the lord of sages, the lord of the gods, remembering the lotus feet of his parents worshipped by all the gods,
Kumara, the guru who grants divine knowledge, reached the peak of Kailasa, surrounded by peaks, shining and supremely wondrous.
Vamadeva too, surrounded by his good disciples, bowing to the one whose mount is the peacock, went quickly to most wondrous Kailasa.
Having made the resolve by the path of the great resolve, "I shall perform the worship of our guru here," he should then touch darbha grass.
Offering his whole body in devotion, forgetting his own frame, he fell down in their presence again and again, and, bowing, rose.
Then with many kinds of hymns, rich in the essence of Veda and Agama, the sage praised the supreme Lord together with Ambika and their son.
Placing the lotus feet of the god and goddess on his own head and receiving their full grace, he dwelt there happily.
You too, knowing thus Maheshvara, the meaning of the pranava, the secret of the Veda, the all, the deliverer, the Brahman that gives liberation,
sit here happily at the feet of Shri Vishveshvara and attain the unequalled, excellent liberation that is union.
I shall go to the hermitage of Badari to serve my guru's lotus feet; may I again have good conversation with you.
Washing their feet and sipping water himself, the performer, silent, should seat them facing east, adorned with ash.
He should meditate on those eight there in the order beginning with Sadashiva, and on the other brahmins too with supreme honour, O sage.
Having given them and adorned them with flowers, with the eight names beginning with the pranava, ending with the dative and "namah," then with fragrant flowers,
giving them mouth-freshener, fees, sandals, seat and leaf-plate, fan, board and bamboo staff,
Agastya, Pulastya, Pulaha and Kratu are your great-souled disciples, Vamadeva, great sage.
Going to the peak of Kailasa and reaching the Lord's presence, the sage beheld the feet of the divine couple, which give liberation and destroy maya.
He should meditate on the Parameshthi guru with the thought of Shiva with Amba, by his own name; then on the supreme guru, and after that on the guru of the high and low.
Saying "This is the seat," he should arrange the seats, uttering his own name beginning with the pranava and in the accusative.
Invoking with "I invoke, namah," with arghya water he should offer water for the feet, sipping water, arghya, garments, fragrance and grains.
Service to the other classes is said to be the dharma of the shudra, as well as making gardens and taking refuge in my holy fields.
For the householder, going to his lawful wife is prescribed; celibacy for forest-dwellers, ascetics and students.
For women, service to the husband is the dharma, and there is no other eternal one; and my worship, auspicious one, if the husband permits it.
Bathing three times, tending the fire, worshipping the linga in due order, giving, the attitude of the Lord, and compassion everywhere and always,
The woman who abandons service to her husband and is devoted to vows goes to hell; there is no need to deliberate on this.
Now I shall tell the eternal dharma of the woman without a husband: vows, giving, austerity, purity, sleeping on the ground, eating at night,
celibacy, bathing always with ash or water, peace, silence, forbearance, and constant sharing according to rule,
and, on the eighth, the fourteenth and especially the full-moon day, and on the eleventh, fasting according to rule and my worship.
Thus in brief I have told the dharma of those who follow the stages of life — of brahmins, kshatriyas and vaishyas, O Goddess, of ascetics and students,
of forest-dwellers and householders, lovely one, of shudras and of women; this is the eternal dharma.
I am always to be meditated upon by you, queen of gods, and the six-syllabled mantra always repeated; this is the whole dharma taught in the Veda, the summary of dharma and its aims.
Now those men in the world who have taken bodies of their own will, endowed with intense feeling and with the impressions of former births,
whether dispassionate or attached, even amid the objects of women and the rest, are not tainted by sins, like a lotus leaf by water.
For them, pure and discerning, who have the knowledge of me as the self, purified by my grace, the keeping of the stages of life is a burden.
